title: Residue groups and multiplication tables
section: Part B: Abstract Algebra ▷ Examples of Groups
terms: additive group modulo n; unit group modulo n; multiplication table; group table; Cayley table.

exposition.text:
The additive group Z/nZ consists of residue classes with addition modulo n, has order n, and is
generated by 1. Multiplication modulo n on all classes is a monoid. Its invertible classes form
∗
(Z/nZ) , whose order is φ(n); a class is invertible exactly when it is coprime to n.
For prime p, every nonzero class is a unit, giving a group of order p − 1. In a group table each
row and each column is a permutation of the elements, by cancellation. Such a table can re-
veal identities and inverses quickly, but the Latin-square property alone does not guarantee
associativity.
To read a Cayley table, use the first factor's row and the second factor's column. The identity
row and column reproduce the headers; the location of the identity in an element's row gives
its right inverse. A symmetric group table indicates commutativity. For composite n, merely re-
moving zero from all residues need not give a group: nonzero zero divisors can destroy closure.

Which group is isomorphic to (Z/8Z) ?
(A) Z/2Z (B) Z/4Z (C) Z/2Z × Z/2Z (D) Z/8Z (E) S
3

solution.text:
The units are 1, 3, 5, 7. Each nonidentity unit squares to 1 modulo 8, so the group has order
four and no element of order four. It is the Klein four-group, not the cyclic group of order
four.

question.text:
∗
How many elements of the unit group (Z/40Z) have order exactly two?
(A) 1 (B) 3 (C) 4 (D) 7 (E) 8

solution.text:
CRT separates modulo forty into modulo eight and modulo five. All four units modulo
eight square to one, while modulo five only 1, −1 do. Hence there are 4 · 2 = 8 roots of
2
u = 1. Every root is a unit, and only the identity has order one, leaving seven elements of
exact order two.

question.text:
For which integers n ≥ 2 do all nonzero residue classes modulo n form a group under multiplica-
tion modulo n?
(A) All n
(B) Exactly the odd n
(C) Exactly the primes
(D) Exactly the prime powers
(E) Exactly the square-free n

solution.text:
For a prime modulus every nonzero class is coprime to the modulus and hence invertible. If
n is composite, write n = ab with 1 < a, b < n. The nonzero classes of a, b multiply to zero,
so the proposed set is not even closed. The full unit group exists for every modulus, but it
can be smaller than the nonzero classes.
